Test a leaf for starch using iodine solution
Explain why each step of the starch test is needed

questions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
questions.a: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis happen in?
questions.a: The chloroplasts.

questions.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.a: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

questions.q: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscles.
questions.a: Lactic acid.

questions.q: Name the two products of fermentation in yeast.
questions.a: Ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Give two factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.a: Any two from: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature.

engage.hook: Potatoes, rice, wheat and a full kitchen cupboard. What do they have in common?
engage.imageDescription: kitchen cupboard full of stored food

reveal.answer: They are all food stores. Plants store food too: the glucose they do not use straight away is kept as starch.

learn.heading: Plants store glucose as starch

items: Photosynthesis makes glucose in the leaves.
Glucose the plant does not need straight away is turned into starch.
Starch is insoluble, so it stays in the cells and can be stored.
At night there is no photosynthesis.
The plant turns starch back into glucose for respiration.
Potatoes, rice and wheat are all starch stores.

learn.imageDescription: potato, rice and wheat as plant starch stores

learn.heading: Variegated leaves

items: Contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
Photosynthesis happens here.
Glucose is made and stored as starch.
No chlorophyll.
No photosynthesis.
No starch is made here.

learn.imageDescription: variegated hosta leaf with green centre and white edges

build.q: What do plants turn spare glucose into so it can be stored?
build.explanation: Spare glucose is stored as starch, mainly in leaves, roots and seeds.

build.q: Why is starch a good way to store glucose?
options: It is insoluble, so it stays in the cells
build.explanation: Starch does not dissolve, so it stays put until the plant needs it.

build.q: Which part of a variegated leaf makes starch?
build.explanation: Only the green part has chlorophyll, so only it photosynthesises and makes starch.

build.q: Why is the leaf put in boiling water first?
options: To kill it and stop its chemical reactions
build.explanation: Boiling kills the leaf, so its reactions stop and it cannot use up its starch.

build.q: Why is the leaf then put in hot ethanol?
build.explanation: Ethanol removes the green chlorophyll, so the iodine colour change is easy to see.

build.q: Why must the Bunsen be off when the ethanol goes into the hot water?
build.explanation: Ethanol catches fire easily, so it is only ever heated in a hot water bath with the flame off.

build.title: Testing a leaf for starch
build.intro: Kill the leaf, remove the chlorophyll, then add iodine to see which parts contain starch.
equipment: Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze and heat-proof mat
steps: Boil the water in the beaker.
Put the leaf in the boiling water for 30 seconds.
Bunsen OFF. Stand the leaf in a tube of ethanol in the hot water for 5 minutes.
Dip the leaf in warm water to soften it.
Spread the leaf flat on the white tile.
Add iodine. Record which parts turn blue-black.
build.warning: Eye protection on. Ethanol is flammable: Bunsen off. Use forceps. Iodine stains skin.
build.imageDescription: four stages of testing a leaf for starch: boiling water, ethanol in water bath, rinsing, iodine on white tile

questions.q: Which parts of your leaf turned blue-black? Explain why.
questions.a: The green parts. They have chlorophyll, so they photosynthesised and stored glucose as starch.

questions.q: Why do you soften the leaf in warm water before adding iodine?
questions.a: Ethanol makes the leaf brittle. Softening lets it lie flat without breaking.

developing.q: Describe the test for starch, including the colour change.
developing.a: Add iodine solution. It turns from orange-brown to blue-black if starch is present.

developing.q: Why do plants store glucose as starch?
developing.a: Starch is insoluble so it stays in the cells. It can be turned back into glucose when the plant needs it.

developing.q: Name three pieces of equipment for the starch test and what each is for.
developing.a: Any three: boiling water kills the leaf; ethanol removes chlorophyll; white tile shows the colour; iodine tests for starch; forceps hold the hot leaf.

reaching.q: Why is the leaf put in ethanol before adding iodine?
reaching.a: Ethanol removes the green chlorophyll, so the blue-black colour is easy to see.

reaching.q: Why is the ethanol heated in a water bath, not over a flame?
reaching.a: Ethanol is flammable. A water bath with the Bunsen off heats it without a flame nearby.

reaching.q: Predict which part of a variegated leaf turns blue-black. Explain why.
reaching.a: The green part. It has chlorophyll, so it photosynthesises and stores glucose as starch. The white part stays orange-brown.

mastering.q: Describe how a leaf makes starch and what a positive starch test looks like.
mastering.a: Chlorophyll absorbs light. Carbon dioxide and water make glucose. Spare glucose is stored as insoluble starch. Iodine turns blue-black.

mastering.q: A plant is kept in the dark for two days. Its leaf stays orange-brown with iodine. Explain why.
mastering.a: No light, so no photosynthesis. The plant turned its stored starch back into glucose for respiration, so none is left.

mastering.q: Describe the four steps of the starch test. Give one risk and how to control it.
mastering.a: Boil leaf; hot ethanol in water bath; soften in warm water; iodine on white tile. Risk: ethanol is flammable, so Bunsen off.
indicativeContent: Boil the leaf in water to kill it and stop its reactions
Turn the Bunsen off, then put the leaf in ethanol in the hot water bath
Soften the leaf in warm water and spread it on a white tile
Risk: ethanol is flammable, so no flame nearby; or hot water burns, so use forceps

cloze: Spare glucose is stored in the leaf as _____.
Starch is _____, so it does not dissolve and stays in the cells.
Hot _____ removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf.
_____ solution turns blue-black when starch is present.

objectives: State Hubble's law and the cosmological principle
Use v = H_0 d to find the speed and distance of a galaxy
Estimate the age of the universe from 1/H_0

questions.q: Write the Doppler equation for light from a moving source.
questions.a: \Delta\lambda / \lambda \approx v / c

questions.q: Light from a distant galaxy is red-shifted. What does this tell you about the galaxy?
questions.a: It is moving away from us (receding).

questions.q: Define one parsec.
questions.a: The distance at which a radius of 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond. About 3.1 × 10^16 m.

questions.q: Define a light-year and give its value in metres.
questions.a: The distance light travels in one year. About 9.5 × 10^15 m.

questions.q: State Wien's displacement law.
questions.a: peak wavelength × T = constant (2.9 × 10^-3 m K)

questions.q: Write Stefan's law and say what L stands for.
questions.a: L = 4\pi r^2 \sigma T^4. L is the luminosity of the star (total power emitted).

specPoints: OCR A 5.5.2 Wien's and Stefan's laws

engage.hook: In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that almost every galaxy is moving away from us. Does that put us at the centre of the universe?
engage.imageDescription: Hubble 1929 velocity-distance graph of nearby galaxies

reveal.answer: No. An observer in any other galaxy would see the same thing. Space itself is expanding, so every galaxy moves away from every other.

learn.heading: What Hubble measured

items: Distance: from standard candles such as Cepheid variable stars.
Recession velocity: from the red shift of its spectral lines, v = c\Delta\lambda/\lambda.
Almost all galaxies are red-shifted, so they are receding.
The further away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes.
The universe is expanding.

learn.imageDescription: absorption spectrum of a galaxy compared with lab spectrum showing red shift

learn.heading: Hubble's law
learn.example: H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. A galaxy 200 Mpc away recedes at v = 70 × 200 = 14 000 km s^-1.
learn.imageDescription: graph of galaxy recession velocity against distance with straight best-fit line through the origin

learn.heading: The Hubble graph

features.label: Straight line through the origin
features.description: v is directly proportional to d

features.label: Gradient
features.description: Equal to the Hubble constant H_0

features.label: Scatter about the line
features.description: Galaxies also have their own local motion

learn.instruction: Sketch the graph and label these features.
learn.imageDescription: Hubble diagram scatter plot of galaxy velocity against distance with best-fit line

learn.heading: The cosmological principle and the age of the universe

items: On a large scale the universe is homogeneous (the same everywhere) and isotropic (the same in every direction).
The laws of physics are the same everywhere.
If the expansion rate has been constant, t \approx 1/H_0.
t \approx 4.4 × 10^17 s \approx 14 billion years.

build.q: Which statement is Hubble's law?
options: Recession velocity is directly proportional to distance
Luminosity is proportional to temperature to the power four
Wavelength of peak emission is inversely proportional to temperature
All galaxies are the same distance from us
build.explanation: v = H_0 d: double the distance, double the recession velocity.

build.q: What is the SI unit of the Hubble constant?
H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. What is the recession velocity of a galaxy 100 Mpc away?
Which observation shows that the universe is expanding?
options: Red shift increases with distance for almost all galaxies
build.explanation: More distant galaxies recede faster, which is what an expanding universe predicts.

build.q: How is the age of the universe estimated from the Hubble constant?
build.explanation: t = d/v = 1/H_0, assuming the expansion rate has been constant.

build.q: The cosmological principle says that on a large scale the universe is:
build.explanation: Same everywhere and the same in every direction, so there is no centre.

build.given: lab \lambda = 656.3 nm, observed \lambda = 669.4 nm, H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1
build.equation: v = c\Delta\lambda ÷ \lambda, then d = v ÷ H_0

questions.q: A galaxy is 350 Mpc away. H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. Calculate its recession velocity.
A galaxy recedes at 1.4 × 10^4 km s^-1. H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. Calculate its distance.
H_0 = 2.3 × 10^-18 s^-1. Estimate the age of the universe in years.

developing.a: The recession velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from us.
On a large scale the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and the laws of physics are the same everywhere.

developing.q: A galaxy is 50 Mpc away. H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. Calculate its recession velocity.

reaching.q: A galaxy recedes at 2.1 × 10^4 km s^-1. H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1. Calculate its distance in Mpc.
Convert H_0 = 70 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 into s^-1. (1 Mpc = 3.1 × 10^22 m)
Explain how the red shift of galaxies is evidence that the universe is expanding.
reaching.a: Almost all galaxies are red-shifted, so receding. Red shift increases with distance, so v \propto d: space is expanding.

mastering.q: A 486 nm line is seen at 510 nm. H_0 = 2.2 × 10^-18 s^-1. Calculate the galaxy's distance in m.
Estimate the age of the universe in years (H_0 = 2.2 × 10^-18 s^-1). State one assumption.
mastering.a: t = 1 ÷ 2.2 × 10^-18 = 4.5 × 10^17 s \approx 1.4 × 10^10 years. Assumes the expansion rate has been constant.

mastering.q: Distant supernovae are further away than their red shift predicts. Suggest what this shows.
mastering.a: The expansion of the universe is accelerating, so galaxies were receding more slowly in the past (linked to dark energy).

meta.title: Renewable Energy Resources and Environmental Factors

objectives: Name the main renewable energy resources
Compare how reliable each resource is and its effect on the environment
Describe and explain trends in how the UK generates electricity

questions.q: Name two non-renewable energy resources.
questions.a: Any two from: coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel.

questions.q: What does non-renewable mean?
questions.a: It will run out. It cannot be replaced as fast as we use it.

questions.q: Name two gases released when coal is burned.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide.

questions.q: Which environmental problem does sulfur dioxide cause?
questions.a: Acid rain.

questions.q: Write the equation for efficiency.
questions.a: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer

questions.q: A kettle has a total input of 2000 J and a useful output of 1600 J. Calculate its efficiency.

specPoints: AQA 4.1.3 National and global energy resources

engage.hook: The UK's last coal power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in September 2024. What is making our electricity instead?
engage.imageDescription: cutaway of a wind turbine showing gearbox and generator

reveal.answer: Mostly gas, nuclear and a fast-growing share of renewables: wind, solar and biofuel. Today we compare the renewables.

learn.heading: Key words

definitions.definition: An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
Available whenever we need it, whatever the weather or time of day.
The carbon dioxide released when it is burned was taken in from the air while the plants grew.

learn.imageDescription: large solar panel array in sunlight

learn.heading: The renewable energy resources

items: Hydroelectric: water falls through a dam and turns turbines.
Tidal and wave: moving sea water turns turbines.
Wind: turbines turn generators.
Solar: cells turn light into electricity; panels heat water.
Geothermal: hot rocks underground heat water to make steam.
Biofuel: plants or animal waste burned for heat, electricity or transport.

learn.imageDescription: geothermal power station with cold water pumped down and steam returning

learn.heading: Reliable or not?

rows.a: Tidal: the tides come in and out twice a day, every day.
Hydroelectric: water is stored behind the dam until needed.
rows.b: Solar: nothing at night, less on cloudy days.

rows.a: Geothermal: the rocks are always hot.
rows.b: Wave: a calm sea makes little electricity.

rows.a: Biofuel: can be stored and burned when demand rises.
rows.b: Unreliable resources need a backup, often gas power stations.

learn.imageDescription: tidal barrage across a river estuary

build.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
build.explanation: Heat from hot rocks is replenished; the others will run out.

build.q: Which renewable resource is the most reliable?
build.explanation: The tides come in and out twice a day, so the output is predictable.

build.q: Which renewable resource releases carbon dioxide when it is used?
build.explanation: Biofuels are burned, which releases carbon dioxide.

build.q: Why are biofuels described as carbon neutral?
options: The carbon dioxide they release was absorbed while the plants grew
They are only burned at night
build.explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, which balances what burning releases.

build.q: Which energy resource can be used for transport as well as electricity?
build.explanation: Biofuels such as bioethanol can fuel cars; the others only make electricity or heat.

build.q: What is the main environmental problem with hydroelectric power?
build.explanation: The dam floods a valley behind it, destroying habitats and farmland.

questions.q: Describe the trend in the use of coal from 2012 to 2017.
questions.a: It fell sharply, from about 143 000 GWh to about 22 000 GWh.

questions.q: Suggest why this trend happened.
questions.a: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Coal power stations closed to cut emissions.

questions.q: Predict what will happen to the renewables line in the future. Explain why.
questions.a: Keep rising: fossil fuels will run out and the UK wants to cut carbon dioxide emissions.

developing.a: Any three from: wind, solar, tidal, wave, hydroelectric, geothermal, biofuel.
Being (or can be) replenished as it is used.

developing.q: Give one reason why wind is not a reliable energy resource.
developing.a: The wind does not always blow, so the output changes.

reaching.q: Explain why biofuels are described as carbon neutral.
reaching.a: The carbon dioxide released when they burn was taken in by the plants for photosynthesis as they grew.

reaching.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of hydroelectric power.
reaching.a: Advantage: reliable, no polluting gases. Disadvantage: floods valleys and destroys habitats; expensive to build.

reaching.q: Explain why solar cells are less useful in the UK than in Spain.
reaching.a: The UK gets less sunlight and more cloud, so solar cells produce less electricity.

mastering.q: Compare tidal and wind power for generating the UK's electricity.
mastering.a: Both renewable, no polluting gases. Tidal is reliable; wind is not. Tidal barrages harm estuary habitats; turbines are a visual eyesore.
indicativeContent: Neither releases carbon dioxide or polluting gases when running
Tidal is reliable: tides happen twice a day and are predictable
Wind is unreliable: output depends on the weather
Tidal barrages are expensive and damage estuary habitats
Wind turbines cause visual pollution and noise
The UK is windy and has a long coastline, so both suit the UK

mastering.q: Iceland uses geothermal power. Explain why southern England cannot easily do the same.
mastering.a: Geothermal needs hot rocks near the surface, near volcanic activity. Southern England has none, so drilling deep enough is too expensive.

mastering.q: A turbine gives 0.6 MW. How many replace a 1200 MW coal station? Why is a backup still needed?
mastering.a: 1200 ÷ 0.6 = 2000 turbines. Wind is unreliable, so a backup such as gas is needed on still days.

objectives: Estimate the area of a surface by counting squares
Calculate the pressure a force makes on a surface
Describe how changing the force or the area changes the pressure

questions.q: What is the unit of pressure?
questions.a: Pascal (Pa), which is the same as N/m^2.

questions.q: What is the unit of force?
questions.a: Newton (N).

questions.q: What is the unit of area?
questions.a: Square metres (m^2) or square centimetres (cm^2).

questions.q: Write the equation that links pressure, force and area.
questions.a: pressure = force ÷ area

questions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
questions.a: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

questions.q: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscles.
questions.a: Lactic acid.

engage.hook: A camel weighs about 5000 N, yet it walks across soft sand without sinking. How?
engage.imageDescription: close-up of a camel's wide flat foot on sand

reveal.answer: Its wide, flat feet spread the weight over a big area. A big area means a small pressure, so it does not sink.

learn.heading: Calculating pressure

components.name: How spread out the force is
The push on the surface, often the weight
The surface the force acts on

rearrangements: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g = 10 N/kg on Earth)
learn.example: A camel has a mass of 500 kg. Weight = 500 × 10 = 5000 N. Its four feet cover 1000 cm^2. Pressure = 5000 ÷ 1000 = 5 N/cm^2.
learn.imageDescription: camel walking on soft desert sand

learn.heading: Estimating area by counting squares

items: Draw around the shape on 1 cm squared paper.
Count every full square.
Count a square as one if more than half of it is inside the line.
Ignore squares less than half inside.
Total number of squares = area in cm^2.

learn.imageDescription: fingerprint outline drawn on centimetre squared paper

learn.heading: Big pressure or small pressure?

rows.a: Bigger force on the same area
rows.b: Smaller force on the same area

rows.a: Same force on a smaller area
rows.b: Same force on a bigger area

rows.a: Drawing pin point, sharp knife, stiletto heel

learn.imageDescription: snowshoes on deep snow next to a drawing pin

build.q: A force in newtons acts on an area in cm^2. What is the unit of the pressure?
build.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area, so the unit is N ÷ cm^2 = N/cm^2.

build.q: A force of 600 N acts on an area of 2 m^2. What is the pressure?
build.explanation: 600 ÷ 2 = 300 Pa. Multiplying (1200) is the common mistake.

build.q: Why do camels have wide feet?
options: To spread their weight over a bigger area and lower the pressure
To increase the pressure on the sand
build.explanation: Same force, bigger area, smaller pressure, so they do not sink.

build.q: The same force pushes on each of these. Which makes the biggest pressure?
options: The point of a drawing pin
build.explanation: The pin point has the smallest area, so the pressure is biggest.

build.q: When you count squares, what do you do with a square that is more than half inside your outline?
options: Count it as half a square
build.explanation: More than half in counts as one; less than half in is ignored.

build.q: In the handprint experiment, what does the newton scale measure?
build.explanation: The scale reads force in newtons. You find the area from the squared paper.

build.title: Handprint pressure
build.intro: Measure the force you push with and the area of your hand, then calculate your hand pressure.
equipment: newton scale (bathroom scale reading in N)
steps: Push down on the newton scale with one hand as hard as you can. Record the force in N.
Draw around the same hand on the squared paper.
Count the squares inside your outline. Count more-than-half squares as one.
The number of squares is the area of your hand in cm^2.
Calculate your hand pressure: pressure = force ÷ area.
Compare your pressure with the rest of the class.
build.warning: Push down steadily. Do not stand or jump on the scale.
build.imageDescription: hand outline drawn on centimetre squared paper next to a newton scale

questions.q: Who in your class had the biggest pressure? Was it because of a bigger force or a smaller hand?
questions.a: Either: a bigger force or a smaller area both give a bigger pressure.

questions.q: Why is counting squares only an estimate of the area?
questions.a: Part squares are rounded to one or zero, so the count is not exact.

reaching.q: Mr Tick has 5 feet. Each foot has an area of 131 cm^2. Calculate the total area of his feet.

Two aliens weigh the same. A has 2 feet, B has 8 feet of the same size. Which makes more pressure, and how many times more?
mastering.a: Alien A. Its feet cover a quarter of the area, so its pressure is 4 times bigger.

mastering.q: Wider tyres stop a tractor sinking into mud. Explain why.
mastering.a: The weight is the same but it is spread over a bigger area, so the pressure on the mud is smaller.
